A database index works like the index at the back of a cookbook. Instead of reading every page to find recipes with potatoes, you look up “potatoes” and go straight to the relevant pages. A database can use an index to find matching rows without checking the whole table.

For example, an index on a customer table’s email column can help the database find a customer by email quickly.

The tradeoff is storage and extra work when data changes. When relevant data is added, updated, or deleted, the database must maintain the index too, which can slow writes. And an index won’t help every query: an email index may do nothing for a search by city.

The new page had more signups because it received twice as many visitors. Its observed conversion rate was actually lower: 160 out of 2,000 visitors, or 8%, compared with 100 out of 1,000, or 10%, for the old page. Those totals don’t establish that the new page converts better, and no significance analysis has been done to assess whether the rate difference could reflect chance.

We don’t yet know whether the reminder emails reduced missed appointments. The rate fell from 18% in August to 12% in September, when reminders began, but the appointment mix and cancellation policy also changed. Without a randomized comparison, this shows an association, not a demonstrated causal effect.

The next useful check is to compare like-for-like appointment types across the two months. If feasible, a test with randomized assignment would help isolate the effect of reminders.

Daily visitor counts include each person once per day; the weekly count includes each person once for the whole week. Someone visiting Monday and Tuesday counts in both daily totals but only once in the weekly total. That’s why adding the daily numbers can give a higher total; it isn’t a reporting error. We should label the views “daily unique visitors” and “weekly unique visitors” to make this clearer.
